title.en: Bretigny of Cayenne: the Governor the Caribs Slew
title.zh: 卡宴總督布雷蒂尼：加勒比人所誅之暴君

texts.period: Carib historical legend of the 17th c.; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Struggles with Early Colonists'

summary.en: Bretigny — man of evil fame — first Governor to Cayenne came. Stern his new ruler, harsh his deeds, for trifling acts the white man bleeds; most cruel was his sway — and the natives, too, he dared to oppress. Then Caribs vowed, in stern redress, that tyrant chief to slay. But Indian women often love the European far above their own red countrymen — and thus Bretigny came to know his danger in Cayenne: soon as, from female lips, he heard the Carib plan, he gave the word to seize all Caribs there. 'Each casts himself into the wave, and in a shark will find his grave, ere bondage he will bear.' The great canoe pursued the swimmers to the shore, and Bretigny, landing, searched until nightfall for an Indian cabin to remain. But the trees have eyes: all night the Carib warriors came noiselessly, and with morning light hundreds of painted warriors appeared, each with his bended bow. Wrapped in his cloak, Bretigny silently stood to meet his fate from Carib hands — by club and arrow there. They slew his guards, raged wherever colonists were found; the Frenchmen came again, but failed — 'tis twenty years ere they prevailed and settled in Cayenne.
summary.zh: 布雷蒂尼——聲名狼藉者——首任卡宴總督也。其治嚴酷，白人以小過見戮，土民亦遭其虐。加勒比人誓誅此暴君。然土女多愛歐人；布雷蒂尼自其口中聞謀，遂下令盡捕加勒比人。眾曰：『寧投波葬鯊腹，不為奴虜！』巨舟追至岸；總督搜至夜宿土屋。林中有目：加勒比戰士徹夜潛行，晨則彩繪武士數百執弓而至。總督裹氈默立，以待其命——棒與箭也。衛兵盡誅，白人村落俱焚；法人再至而不成——二十年後始得定居卡宴。

sensitivity.note: Carib historical legend recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; a colonial-era conflict narrative, read critically.

passages.text: Bretigny — man of evil fame — first Governor to Cayenne came. Frenchmen were there before, living as Indians there in peace, their wives and language Caribisce, thinking of France no more. Stern their new ruler, harsh his deeds, for trifling acts the white man bleeds; most cruel was his sway. The natives, too, he dared oppress. Then Caribs vowed, in stern redress, that tyrant chief to slay!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Struggles with Early Colonists'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But Indian women often love the European far above their own red countrymen — and thus Bretigny came to know his danger in Cayenne. Soon as, from female lips, he heard the Carib plan, he gave the word to seize all Caribs there. 'Each casts himself into the wave, and in a shark will find his grave, ere bondage he will bear.' Swim now, ye Caribs, for your lives! That great canoe can swiftly run; her crew have halberd, sword, and gun — all Frenchmen, strong and bold!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Struggles with Early Colonists'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They gain the shore. Then, in pursuit, Bretigny lands, searches there, and finds an Indian cabin where he may all night remain. Ah! little does Bretigny know the tactics of an Indian foe: the trees have eyes to see where he abides, and all the night the Carib warriors, armed for fight, are coming noiselessly. With morning light they all appear, hundreds of painted warriors near, each with his bended bow. Wrapped in his cloak, he silent stands to meet his fate from Carib hands, by club and arrow there. They slay his guards, then rage around wherever colonists are found, destroying all white men. The Frenchmen come again, but fail; 'tis twenty years ere they prevail and settle in Cayenne.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Struggles with Early Colonists'; not verbatim.

region.en: From Marowijne to the Orinoco headwaters
region.zh: 馬羅維恩至奧里諾科上游

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Warlike Legends: The Carib War Path'

summary.en: The way they marched to all was known: custom had made that track their own. 'Twas to those rovers mere child's play to plunder there, sometimes to slay, and often to enslave. Their large canoes were often seen as they sailed round from Marowijne and Surinam to Corentyne, then towards that river's head; above the falls they cross Berbice, and march where all is perfect peace. That region they have swept quite bare, and all the people who lived there are captive, slain, or fled. O'er Essequibo then they go: plunder Macusis, or, below, sweep the Brazilian plain; or towards the Pacaraima chain bend their course. On rafts concealed they float near shore, with grass or branches covered o'er; sometimes on fallen trees they glide, such as come downward with the tide. Woe to the victims they surprise! All adults slain, each girl a prize must in their hands remain.
summary.zh: 加勒比人之征路，人所共知；沿俗而行，劫殺虜掠，如兒戲耳。巨舟自馬羅維恩、蘇利南至科倫丁，復溯其源；越灘而渡伯比斯，行於至靜之地——其地之民，或虜或戮或逃，蕩然無餘。復越埃斯塞基博，掠馬庫希，或南掃巴西之原，或向帕卡賴馬之山。藏筏草蔽而近岸；或乘浮木隨潮而進。遭其突者禍矣：成人盡戮，女子盡為戰利。

sensitivity.note: Carib raiding tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; read critically — a colonizer's versification of intertribal warfare.

title.en: The War on the Orinoco: the Cabres and the Ten Thousand
title.zh: 奧里諾科之戰：卡布雷與萬人之師

region.zh: 卡羅尼河與奧里諾科灘

texts.period: Carib historical legend; recorded 1880 (Brett, after Humboldt)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'The War on the Orinoco'

summary.en: Now when they reach Caroni's banks they find additions to their ranks — all come to fight the Cabre race, in Cabre blood wash out disgrace, and thus avenge their dead. By desultory fights enraged, both sides in earnest had engaged: the Cabres made their clans unite under one leader for that fight, and dealt a deadly blow — the Caribs, who till then believed themselves invincible, received a total overthrow. One who survived was forced to climb a tree that thence he might the better see the savage victors eat the slain, and there the wretch had to remain till morning; the chieftain Tep released him then, and bade him bring his countrymen for food some other day. Ah! better had the victors spared that horrid deed and taunt, which, heard, inspired with deadly hate their foe. They vowed, and had it in their power, their strength increasing every hour — allies by hundreds came — until ten thousand men, they say, the Caribs mustered for the fray to wipe away their shame. In deadly fight they met again; the Caribs victors were. Soon as that grim fight was done, extermination was begun: the conquering Caribs then could go where Orinoco's torrents flow — from those falls to ocean's wave, no living foe was found.
summary.zh: 加勒比至卡羅尼之岸，諸部來會——皆欲滅卡布雷之族，以血洗恥。卡布雷合諸部於一帥，大破加勒比——素以不敗自居者，竟全軍覆沒。一倖存者被迫登樹，目睹勝者食敵屍，竟夜不得下；晨，酋長特普釋之，且令他日再送族人為食。此暴行與譏言，激其死仇。盟友千百而至，末集萬人，以雪前恥。再戰，加勒比勝；戰罷即行滅族。其人遂可縱橫奧里諾科之灘——自灘至海，無一生敵。

sensitivity.note: Carib historical legend recorded by Brett 1880 after Humboldt; Brett notes the surviving Guiana Caribs deny cannibalism except as a threat, and Humboldt acquits the continental Caribs while blaming the Cabres — the record keeps both claims visible and read critically.

By desultory fights enraged, both sides in earnest had engaged. The Cabres made their clans unite under one leader for that fight, and dealt a deadly blow: the Caribs, who till then believed themselves invincible, received a total overthrow!

passages.text: But there is one who remembers well, who has been spared that he may tell of the succeeding night. He then was forced to climb a tree, that thence he might the better see the savage victors eat the slain; and there the wretch had to remain till morning, legends say. The chieftain, Tep, released him then, and bade him 'bring his countrymen for food some other day.' Ah! better had the victors spared that horrid deed and taunt, which, heard, inspired with deadly hate their foe, who vowed to strike a mortal blow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The War on the Orinoco'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At length ten thousand men, they say, the Caribs mustered for the fray, to wipe away their shame. In deadly fight they met again; each meant to conquer or be slain — the Caribs victors were. Their fury nothing could withstand; they fought, and perished there. Their warriors then in battle fell: and stern the fate, as legends tell, of all who bore their name. For, soon as that grim fight was done, extermination was begun. The conquering Caribs then could go where Orinoco's torrents flow — returning home, each Carib brave would pass by many a bloody grave: but, from those falls to ocean's wave, no living foe was found!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The War on the Orinoco'; not verbatim.

title.en: The First People: Mankind Descends to Cleanse the World

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Mythological Legends of the Ancient World: The First People'

summary.en: From on high mankind descended: not, as some would say, for food; they came to cleanse this world intended, that it might be fair and good, bright and free from soil or stain, as the moon or starry train. While they toiled, the clouds receded which had borne them from on high; vainly for their help they pleaded — none restored them to the sky. Thus mankind remained below, in a world of toil and woe. As they wandered, pangs of hunger forced them clayey earth to take; which, that they might starve no longer, making fire, they tried to bake — but their cakes, when they were 'done', were like sand, or crumbling stone. Tamosi had there provided wild fruits, suiting beast or bird; by those creatures kindly guided to the trees which each preferred, men partook — but still would sigh for the food they left on high.
summary.zh: 初民自高天而降——非為覓食，乃欲滌此世，使如日月星辰之皎潔無瑕。方其勤作，載其下降之雲漸退；呼援無應，遂不得復歸於天。人間於是惟勤與苦。行乞於野，饑甚，採黏土燒之為餅；熟則如沙如礫。塔莫西已備野果，各宜其獸鳥；眾賴其引至各愛之樹而食——然猶思天上来之饌而歎焉。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose.

title.en: The First Cultivation: Tamosi Kabo-tano's Wondrous Tree
title.zh: 初耕：塔莫西卡博塔諾之神樹

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'The First Cultivation'

summary.en: Tamosi, the Mighty Maker (whom no mortal eye can see) — Tamosi Kabo-tano, 'Ancient one of Heaven', the Supreme Being — made, that man might be partaker of His gifts, a wondrous tree. High o'er all its head uprearing, cloudlike mass of brilliant green; on its noble branches bearing fruits which none before had seen; each a different kind would bear. Lower down, its trunk surrounding, plantains grew, bananas sweet; golden maize waved its plumy tresses there; sweet cassava, with the bitter, beneath the fruits; yams, potatoes, every kind, where widely spread its mighty roots: there was found, in pristine state, all that men now cultivate. 'Twas Maipuri, the tapir, from the river's margin coming, who observed it first of all, daily through the forest stealing, devouring its fruits which fell, its existence still concealing. Men, who saw him fat and sleek, sent forth scouts the truth to seek: first Woodpecker, who kept tapping each old tree from long habit — shrewd Maipuri heard him rapping and went another way; but the Rat, with silent toil, tracked his steps, then shared the spoil — till some food, delicious, sticking to his lips was found, and mankind made him show that feeding ground. All exclaimed: 'O noble tree! Precious gift of Tamosi!' Then an oracle commanded: 'Cut it down!' — they wondered all; yet sharp stones, as fate demanded, caused it in ten months to fall; crashing, thundering to the ground, while they fly or tremble round. Then, a fair division making, for his field each man provides, slips and cuttings freely taking from its branches, roots, and sides: 'Gaining thus at once precious fruits and daily bread.'
summary.zh: 塔莫西卡博塔諾——『天上之古者』，至尊也——欲分其賜於人，乃造神樹。其冠如翠雲，高聳入雲；枝結人所未見之果，各各不同；樹幹四圍生蕉與甜薯，金黃玉蜀黍飄其穗；甘苦二薯、山藥、馬鈴薯，凡今人所耕者，皆具於其巨根之間。貘自河濱來，先見之；日日潛林食落果，秘而不宣。人見其肥，遣偵察之：啄木鳥叩木如常，貘聞聲而改道；田鼠無聲躡其跡，分其食——口黏美饌，眾乃逼其獻樹。眾呼曰：『偉哉此樹！塔莫西之珍賜也！』神諭令伐；以利石伐之，十閱月而樹仆。各取其枝、根、側之苗而分植——『果與日糧，一舉而兩得。』

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Variant of the food-tree records.

passages.text: Tamosi, the Mighty Maker (whom no mortal eye can see), made, that man might be partaker of His gifts, a wondrous tree. Though on earth huge trees have grown, none like that was ever known. High o'er all its head uprearing, cloudlike mass of brilliant green! On its noble branches bearing fruits, which none before had seen: each a different kind would bear, beauteous clusters, high in air! Lower down — its trunk surrounding — plantains grew, bananas sweet: all choice plants were there abounding which we now in gardens meet.

title.en: The Rock and the Wood: the Oracle, the Monkey, and the Flood
title.zh: 石與林：神諭、靈猴與洪水

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'The Rock and the Wood'

summary.en: 'Neath the roots of that great tree some a sacred grot could see. Saw they there the Water-Mother bathing in her loved abode? That it was her form, none other, soon the swelling waters showed: men had all been swept away by a gushing flood that day — but a rugged rock, befriending, closed the fountain; and drew near that rock, which then gave forth oracles to men, saying: 'Though I from the waters save you, there may come a day when yourselves, your sons and daughters, in a flood will pass away. Listen, then, mankind, to me, that your years like mine may be. In yon wood are spirits dwelling, who will tempt you day by day. If you dread the waters swelling, answer not, whate'er they say! You are safe while you obey, heeding well your rock-stone grey. And if age bring evils on you — wrinkled skin and whitening hair — you at will may cast them from you, youth renewing, bright and fair: as the serpent glideth clear from the slough he scorns to wear!' Time has passed; deteriorating, men grow careless day by day, till their hearts, long hesitating, voices from the wood obey. From the grove comes, beguiling, Yarrekaru, the monkey; none prevent him while, alone, he undermines their guardian stone. From the grove come, mockingly, cries of 'Waters cover me!' They respond: 'O friend, we hear them!' laugh, and turn to slumber on — till the rush of waters near them terrifies the stoutest one. And these words, in solemn tone, issue from the outraged stone: 'Lo! the swelling floods before you; I no more your help can be. Yet had you but faithful been, death no man would e'er have seen!' Swell the mighty floods; yet to three or four is given safety till the floods subside, for a komoo palm surmounts the tide: all whom that tree does not save sink, as rocks, beneath the wave — and there is an episode of a cocorite palm whose top reached the heavens: a poor woman led the way halfway up, was turned into stone by terror and exhaustion, and all who tried to pass over her became rocks likewise.
summary.zh: 神樹根下有聖穴；見水母浴於其所居乎！水面暴漲，乃知其形。洪水將盡沒眾人——一巨石忽塞其泉，石遂出神諭：『我救爾於水，然爾與爾之子孫終有滅於洪之日。聽我言，可如我之長年。林中有鬼，日日誘爾；水漲之聲起，慎勿應答！守我灰石則安。老至而皺髮白者，可自脫之，復為青春——如蛇之蛻皮也！』久而人懈，聽林中之聲，忽其灰石。林中遣猴雅雷卡魯來，無人阻之，獨掘其守石。夜聞林中笑呼：『水沒我矣！』眾應曰：『友乎，我聞之矣！』笑而入睡——俄而水聲近，壯者亦懼。石憤而言：『洪水已至，我不能救；爾若忠信，世無見死之人！』洪水滔天；惟三四人攀天生之孔摩棕而免，餘者如石而沉——更有柯基里棕之插曲：其顛及天，一孕婦先登，半途驚疲化石，後攀者越之者亦皆化石。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Flood-cluster record.

From the grove come, mockingly, cries of 'Waters cover me!' They respond: 'O friend, we hear them!' laugh, and turn to slumber on — till the rush of waters near them terrifies the stoutest one. passages.text: Yet had you but faithful been, death no man would e'er have seen!' Swell the mighty floods, prevailing — yet to three or four is given safety till the floods subside, for a komoo palm (by heaven made to grow) surmounts the tide: all whom that tree does not save sink, as rocks, beneath the wave. There is an episode, usually given here, of a cocorite palm whose top reached the heavens: a poor woman, not in a condition to climb, led the way, and halfway up was turned into stone by terror and exhaustion; none could help her, and all who tried to pass over her became rocks likewise.

narrative.en: The Carib cycle of Tamosi Kabo-tano — 'the Ancient One of Heaven', the Supreme Being — reaches its crisis in the legend of the Rock and the Wood. Under the roots of the wonderful tree from which all cultivated plants first came, some saw a sacred grotto, and in it the Water-Mother bathing in her loved abode; that it was her form none other, the swelling waters soon showed, for a gushing flood burst out that would have swept all mankind away — had not a rugged rock, by what power none can know, closed the fountain. The people drew near to their saviour, and the rock gave forth oracles: 'Though I from the waters save you, there may come a day when yourselves, your sons and daughters, in a flood will pass away. Listen, then, mankind, to me, that your years like mine may be. In yon wood are spirits dwelling, who will tempt you day by day. If you dread the waters swelling, answer not, whate'er they say! You are safe while you obey, heeding well your rock-stone grey. And if age bring evils on you — wrinkled skin and whitening hair — you at will may cast them from you, youth renewing, bright and fair, as the serpent glideth clear from the slough he scorns to wear.' Thus the rock offered both the covenant of safety and the serpent's gift of skin-renewal, the Guianese form of earthly immortality. Time passed; men grew careless, and their hearts, long hesitating, obeyed the voices from the wood. From the grove came Yarrekaru, the monkey, sent by man's malignant foes; none prevented him while, alone, he undermined their guardian stone. From the grove came mockingly the cries of 'Waters cover me!' — the people answered 'O friend, we hear them!', laughed, and turned to slumber on, until the rush of waters near them terrified the stoutest. The outraged stone spoke in solemn tone: 'Lo! the swelling floods before you; I no more your help can be. Yet had you but faithful been, death no man would e'er have seen!' The floods prevailed, and death returned to the world with them. Only three or four survived on a komoo palm that heaven made to grow above the tide; all the rest sank like rocks beneath the wave — for in the usual episode of the cycle, those who strove to climb the cocorite palm, whose top reached the heavens, found the way blocked by a poor woman turned to stone by terror and exhaustion halfway up, and every climber who tried to pass over her became rock likewise. The tale is told by the Rev. W. H. Brett in metrical form from Carib informants of British Guiana, and its imagery — the guardian stone, the tempting wood, the tree whose crown reaches the sky, the serpent's skin — binds the Guianese flood cycle to the wider American pattern of the broken covenant and the second creation.

functions: Flood-and-covenant myth: the guardian rock's oracle establishes the pact of obedience whose breach restores death to the world
Explains standing rocks and stones as the petrified dead of the deluge, and names the komoo palm as the ark of the Carib remnant
Locates the serpent-skin renewal — sloughing as youth-renewal — in the same moral field as the covenant, joining origin-of-death to origin-of-taboo
Legitimises the siesta of fear: the voices from the wood are real, and the tale teaches silence in their season

variants.name: Akawai version (Brett, 'The Monkey's Exploit')
variants.summary: The flood issues from the stump of the wonderful tree itself and is checked by an inverted basket until the mischief-making monkey raises it; the survivors climb a hill of cocorite palms and rocks near Roroima.

variants.name: Arawak version (Brett, 'The Fire and the Flood')
variants.summary: Fire came first, foretold by the Maker, and survivors hid in a sand-roofed pit on a reef; the flood followed, and Marerewana moored his canoe by a long bush-rope to a great tree.

variants.name: Taulipang version (Koch-Grünberg)
variants.summary: The world-tree Wazakä is felled with magic words; its stump is the Roroima, and the basket over the stump is lifted by Makunaima's impatience, releasing the flood from which each brother climbs an Inajä palm.

title.en: Amalivaca Carves the Rocks and Tames the Rivers (Brett Version)
title.zh: 阿馬利瓦卡刻石馴河（布雷特版）

texts.period: Tamanac-Carib tradition recorded by Humboldt; versified 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Legend of Amalivaca'

summary.en: While the deluge was subsiding from some land of unknown name, over the mighty waters gliding, great Amalivaca came, sailing on where now are seen widespread plains and forests green. Doubtless sent our race to raise, helping men in many ways. In the sculptures so high on the rocks his work you see: waters at that height were flowing, so he carved them easily, carved them from his great canoe, taught mankind to carve them too — each device and time-worn figure had, of old, its well-known lore, voiceless all, they spake with vigour to the eye in days of yore; but our wisest all allow none can read their lessons now. When the mighty floods were failing and the land again was seen, wildly rugged all the ground then Amalivaca found; but his brother gave assistance, and by that good brother's aid, overcoming all resistance, smooth and gentle slopes he made. Men asked him for canoes and streams: 'But when we pass the tidal power, going up no help is found. Now exert thy wondrous skill — strive to remedy this ill.' Then he spent much toil and trouble on great Orinoco's flood, and strove to make its current double: one side up, the other down. Orinoco answered 'No!' Then he strove the tides of ocean to the upper stream to bring; but the river said: 'You seek a fatal thing: if the tide should higher go, all will be submerged below!' This Amalivaca learned; and from fruitless labour turned — and from that time nevermore comes he to this Western shore. Humboldt considers those rock-carvings to be traces of an ancient civilisation.
summary.zh: 洪水將退，阿馬利瓦卡自異邦乘巨舟而來，行於今之平原綠林之上。蓋為興我族、濟眾生而至。高崖之刻畫，即其手澤——其時水至彼處，故自舟中刻之甚易；且教人亦刻。古之圖形各有其義，今之智者亦莫能讀矣。水退地見，丘壑叢雜；其弟助之，平為緩坡。人求通舟之川；告以潮之難；彼欲使奧里諾科上下同流——河曰『否』！又欲引海潮上溯——河曰：『此取死之道：潮高則下皆沒矣！』阿馬利瓦卡乃知水非其造者莫能改，遂罷。臨去，眾揮淚送舟；自此不復西來。洪堡謂崖刻乃古文明之遺跡云。

sensitivity.note: Tamanac tradition recorded by Humboldt, versified by Brett 1880; paraphrased into prose. Variant of the amalivaca-orinoco record.

passages.text: While the deluge was subsiding from some land of unknown name, o'er the mighty waters gliding, great Amalivaca came — sailing on where now are seen widespread plains and forests green. Ocean waves he had crossed over, sailing in his large canoe; from that other side a rover, seeking lands and people new: doubtless sent our race to raise, helping men in many ways.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Amalivaca'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the sculptures I am showing, now so high, his work you see! Waters at that height were flowing, so he carved them easily — carved them from his great canoe, taught mankind to carve them too. Each device and time-worn figure had, of old, its well-known lore: voiceless all, they spake with vigour to the eye in days of yore; but our wisest all allow none can read their lessons now. When the mighty floods were failing and the land again was seen, wildly rugged all the ground then Amalivaca found; but his brother gave assistance, and by that good brother's aid, overcoming all resistance, smooth and gentle slopes he made.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Amalivaca'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'But when a canoe is bearing, heavy burdens light become' — the men said: 'When we pass the tidal power, going up no help is found; heavy is the work each hour. Now exert thy wondrous skill — strive to remedy this ill.' Then he spent much toil and trouble on great Orinoco's flood, and strove to make its current double: one side up, the other down. Orinoco answered: 'No!' Then he strove the tides of ocean to the upper stream to bring; but the river, with emotion, said: 'You seek a fatal thing: if the tide should higher go, all will be submerged below!' This Amalivaca learned; and from fruitless labour turned — and from that time nevermore comes he to this Western shore. When the black-robed teachers found us, we inquired if they had seen him who left such marks around us — and we grieved when all said 'No!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Amalivaca'; not verbatim.

title.en: Manarowa and the Falls: the Carib Chief and the Amphibious Race
title.zh: 馬納羅瓦與瀑：加勒比酋長與兩棲之族

region.zh: 蓋亞那埃斯塞基博瀑（曼德羅瓦瀑）

texts.period: Carib historical legend of the 18th-19th c.; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Legend of Manarowa'

summary.en: Sweet is his Essequibo home; yet still Manarowa will roam to gain more power and fame: from Orinoco to Corentyne fighting and plundering he has been — the Indians round him own his sway, and slaves, as tribute, to him pay: all, save the Taruma. They on that stream above are found; but he, to reach them, must go round, ascending the Rewa — for the great Essequibo Falls, never yet passed, like mighty walls, confront Manarowa. 'Those Tarumas we must invade, and take them by surprise: o'er those grim cataracts we will haul our light canoes, and on them fall, as coming from the skies!' He scaled one wat'ry wall where a small island in the fall gave precarious footing; then, no footing to be found, 'We now must clear a pathway through the forest here, and drag our vessels round.' Thus they, still toiling day by day, o'er falls and rapids worked their way — and the rocks are high, the Caribs nigh, no power is theirs to fight or fly: the Tarumas hid themselves and woodskins in caverns deep beneath the tide, and thus eluded the chase. 'Have we thus far come through such perils to make war on an amphibious race?' The tale had to a legend grown, of that amphibious race eluding him who ventured o'er a path no mortal man before, or after, dared to trace — for near one hundred years, until a white explorer, Mr. C. B. Brown in 1870, crossed o'er every dangerous fall, giving that highest, worst of all its name — Mandrowa. And when Great Britain put down the slave-trade his business was gone: small-pox and rum consumed his clan; he saw them dying man by man, grieved, and his spirit fled.
summary.zh: 馬納羅瓦之埃斯塞基博家園固美，然彼猶四出以求權名：自奧里諾科至科倫丁，戰而掠之；四周部落皆臣，貢以奴隸——惟塔魯馬不臣。欲達之，必遡雷瓦河而上——蓋埃斯塞基博大瀑未嘗有人過者，如牆當道。酋曰：『當突襲塔魯馬：曳輕舟過惡灘，自天而降！』攀一瀑而藉小嶼立足；再遇無立足者，遂曰：『當闢林徑，曳舟繞行。』日日力作，越灘而行——然兩棲之族匿其身與皮舟於潮下深穴，蹤跡遂失。酋歎曰：『歷此萬險，乃與兩棲之族戰乎？』此事百年成為傳說——至1870年白人探險家布朗越諸瀑，名最高最險者為曼德羅瓦瀑。英國禁奴販，其業遂盡；天花與朗姆滅其族——目睹族人相繼死，憂憤而亡。

sensitivity.note: Carib historical legend recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; a colonial-era chief narrative, read critically.

passages.text: Sweet is his Essequibo home; yet still Manarowa will roam to gain more power and fame. Though, from that river's sources south to Dutch plantations near its mouth, the tribes all fear his name: from Orinoque to Corentyne, fighting and plundering he has been — the bold Manarowa! The Indians round him own his sway, and slaves, as tribute, to him pay: all, save the Taruma. They on that stream above are found; but he, to reach them, must go round, ascending the Rewa — for the great Essequibo Falls, never yet passed, like mighty walls, confront Manarowa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Manarowa'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief has pondered long, and said: 'Those Tarumas we must invade, and take them by surprise. O'er those grim cataracts we will haul our light canoes, and on them fall, as coming from the skies!' Now he has scaled one watery wall, where a small island in the fall precarious footing gave. With toil they hoist and carry o'er their craft. With that great fall they scarce have done, ere they come to a greater one: no footing there is found. 'We now must clear a pathway through the forest here, and drag our vessels round.' Thus they, still toiling day by day, o'er falls and rapids work their way with labour most severe.

passages.text: The rocks are high, the Caribs nigh, no power is theirs to fight or fly: the Tarumas themselves and woodskins now hide in caverns deep beneath the tide, and thus elude our chase! 'Have we thus far come through such perils to make war on an amphibious race?' To all on Essequibo known, the tale had to a legend grown, of that amphibious race eluding him who ventured o'er a path no mortal man before, or after, dared to trace — for near one hundred years, until a white explorer crosses, o'er every dangerous fall, giving that highest, worst of all its name — Mandrowa. And when Great Britain put down the slave-trade, his business was gone: small-pox and rum consumed his clan; he saw them dying, man by man; grieved, and his spirit fled!
